newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian hostages released in Chechnya.
newsitem.headline: Russian hostages released in Chechnya.

text.p: Rebel field commander Salman Raduyev, under heavy pressure from Chechnya's separatist leaders, freed Russian policemen on Wednesday he had held hostage since Saturday.

But the situation in the breakaway region, which is preparing to elect a new president and parliament on January 27, remained tense with most international aid agencies pulling out after the murder of six foreign aid workers there on Tuesday.

Reporters who were taken by Raduyev's fighters to their headquarters in the village of Novye Gordali became the first to tell 21 Russians and one policemen from the Dagestan region bordering Chechnya the news they were about to be freed.
The 22 men were offered a meal in the rebels' canteen while Raduyev and Kremlin envoy Boris Berezovsky signed documents on their release. The policemen looked nervous but otherwise fine.
After the signing the hostages were taken to the village of Gerzel-Kutan on the Dagestani border 10 km (7 miles) away, handed over to the Russians and flown off by helicopter.
Raduyev's fighters disarmed and seized the policemen on Saturday when they tried to prevent them from entering Dagestan.

Top separatist officials, keen to end an incident that threatened to upset Chechnya's fragile peace process and planned local elections, had promised to force Raduyev to release all his hostages unconditionally.
But Raduyev refused to follow the orders of the separatist government for four days, saying he wanted apologies from Russia for not letting him visit Dagestan.
"There had been pressure on Raduyev from all sides, from both Chechen and Russian officials, to free the policemen," Interior Ministry Vladimir Vorozhtsov told Reuters in Moscow.
Russian television said Berezovsky had promised to free 11 Chechen fighters from Russian prisons in exchange for the policemen. This report could not be immediately confirmed.

Earlier on Wednesday Interfax news agency quoted Russia's Deputy Interior Minister Vladimir Kolesnikov as saying Russian police had stepped up efforts to investigate another incident overshadowing Chechnya's shaky peace process.

Unidentified masked gunmen entered a compound of the Geneva- based International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) in the village of Novye Atagi and shot dead six workers of the relief agency who helped to run a local hospital.

The six came from Norway, the Netherlands, Canada, Spain and New Zealand. A seventh worker, a Swiss who ran the project, was wounded. The survivor and the bodies of the six were flown to Geneva on Wednesday.
"We have good reason to believe that in the near future it will become clear who committed this crime," Kolesnikov said in Moscow. No one has claimed responsibility for the attack.
Following the killing of the relief workers international aid agencies began pulling out of Chechnya on Wednesday.

Aleth Jaurou from the North Caucasus mission of Medecins sans Frontieres (MSF) told Reuters that her agency was suspending activities in Chechnya in solidarity with the ICRC. She could not say how long the suspension would last.
MSF workers were among the first to land in Chechnya after Russia sent troops there in December 1994 to quell the region's independence drive.

The ICRC said on Tuesday it was withdrawing all its international staff, leaving local staff to look after the Novye Atagi hospital and other Chechnya relief offices. The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees and Paris-based medical charity Medecins du Monde also scaled back their work.

In an unrelated incident reported by Interfax on Wednesday, authorities in another north Caucasus region, North Ossetia, said three senior officials had been kidnapped in Chechnya by gunmen seeking a $6 million ransom.
The kidnapping did not appear to be politically motivated.
Kidnappings for ransom have become frequent in Chechnya where armed groups which fought against Russia in the war are jobless after a peace deal struck on August 31.
